title: Tale of the Market Dreamer
summary: In a crowded quarter of Cairo lived an idle young man named Bakkar who refused to learn a trade, preferring to spend his pennies on herbal smoke that induced vivid, waking dream...
full_text:
In a crowded quarter of Cairo lived an idle young man named Bakkar who refused to learn a trade, preferring to spend his pennies on herbal smoke that induced vivid, waking dreams. One sultry afternoon, he sat upon a stone bench before an ancient public fountain, closed his eyes, and drifted into an elaborate reverie.

In his dream, he was no longer an impoverished beggar in patched wool, but the Grand Sultan of the Orient! He rode through the gates on a magnificent Arabian steed caparisoned in velvet and pearls. Heralds blew silver trumpets, courtiers bowed to the dust, and crowds showered him with rose petals and gold coin.

Entering the royal palace, he ascended the throne of ivory and gold. He summoned his treasurer and commanded a million dinars to be distributed among the poor of Cairo. He ordered forty ships to set sail for the Spice Islands and decreed a feast of roasted peacocks for the whole city. Then, imagining his royal guards stood before him awaiting his command to march upon his enemies, he shouted aloud with royal majesty: 'Charge! Spare none who oppose my will!'

Lost in his delusion, Bakkar leaped from the stone bench, flailed his arms wildly, and dove headfirst into the public fountain! The icy water instantly shattered his dream. He spluttered, choked on fountain moss, and scrambled out into the street drenched from head to foot, his turban floating away in the gutter.

A crowd of laughing washerwomen and schoolboys gathered round, clapping their hands at the dripping 'Sultan' who had conquered nothing but a horse-trough. Shivering with cold and burning with shame, Bakkar realized that illusions provide a moment of mock majesty at the cost of enduring dignity. From that afternoon, he threw away his herbs, took an apprenticeship with a cooper, and discovered the genuine satisfaction of an honest day's labor.
moral: Chasing artificial illusions weakens the spirit; true happiness is built on clear-headed reality.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Tale of the Hashish Eater"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
